title: The mobile visit for a recruiting firm
metaTitle: The mobile visit for a recruiting firm
excerpt: On a phone, the first screen still has to name the kind of role and offer a way to brief the search. Do not let the desktop layout decide it.
alt: Three hands holding coffee cups together over a wooden table, two with latte art, a meeting ritual that should not replace the role on a phone screen.
caption: A toast of cups is a meeting, not the seat you fill. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must the first phone screen of a recruiting site show?
faqs.answer: The kind of role you fill, and a way to brief the search, without scrolling. The button should use a short label a thumb can hit. A candidate link can exist as text. It should not sit as a second button of equal weight.

faqs.question: Which speed measures matter on that first screen?
faqs.answer: Google's good thresholds are a Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, an Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds, and a Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. web.dev describes those as loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. A hero that jumps or arrives late spends the opening seconds on the wrong problem.

faqs.question: Should the desktop design be finished first?
faqs.answer: No. Write and stack the phone view first, then let the wide screen add space around the same words. A desktop poster that gets cropped will hide the role sentence. If a headline only works on a wide monitor, it is the wrong headline.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A recruiting firm mobile website is where most hiring managers will judge you. The first screen still has to show the kind of role you fill and a way to brief the search. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page. A wide hero that crops the role sentence into a fragment has already failed the person holding the phone between meetings.

Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats three measures as the bar for a page that feels stable: Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. web.dev describes those same measures as loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. On a phone, all three show up as trust. A headline that arrives late, a button that waits, or a layout that jumps when a font loads will be read as carelessness. A hiring manager who has been burned is already looking for carelessness.

## Design the phone before the wide screen

Start the layout at a narrow width. Write the role sentence so it fits in the first view without depending on a crop. Put the brief where a thumb can reach it. Then let the desktop version add space around that same stack. The reverse, shrinking a desktop poster until it fits, is how the role disappears and the handshake remains.

Open the page on a phone you did not design on. Read only what is visible before any scroll. You should be able to say the kind of role and see how to brief the search. If you have to scroll to find either, the desktop composition won. Move the sentence up. Cut the eyebrow line that says "boutique retained search" if it pushes the role below the fold.

A meeting photograph, three cups on a table, a lobby, can wait below. It is not the first screen. The first screen is a sentence and an action. The picture can support them if it still shows the role after the crop. If the meaningful part of the picture is at the edge, it will be gone on a phone. Choose a frame whose subject is in the center, or do not use that frame as the hero.

Keep the type large enough to read without pinching. A role sentence set for a desktop column becomes a caption on a phone if you only scale the layout. Set a minimum size and let the sentence wrap. Wrapping is better than a line the buyer cannot read at arm's length.

## The brief has to be in the first view

The action is "Brief a search," or whatever honest verb you use, and it has to be visible with the role. A text link in a menu is not enough if the menu is closed. Put a button in the first view. You can repeat it after the method. You should not hide the only copy under a tall image.

The button label has to fit on one line at that width. "Brief a search" fits. "Begin a confidential consultation with our partners" does not. The long promise can live on the next screen. The button is the door.

Do not place a second button beside it for candidates. On a phone, two buttons of equal weight become the whole screen. Give candidates a text link. Give the buyer the button. A hiring manager who has been burned will assume a split screen means you are a job board that also charges fees.

If the button sticks to the bottom as they scroll, keep it short and do not let it cover the sentence they are reading. A sticky bar that hides the last line of a proof is a tax. Test it on a small phone, not only on a large one. The smallest screen you care about is the one to design for.

## What to cut when the width shrinks

The phone page is not a smaller copy of every desktop block. Cut, in this order.

A logo wall. It becomes a smear. An autoplay video. It burns the loading budget and often starts with a handshake. A five-column process. It becomes a long scroll of identical steps. A paragraph of origin story above the role. It spends the only screen you are likely to get.

Keep the role, the brief, one picture that survives the crop, one refusal, and one path into a proof story. The fee shape can be a single sentence with a link in ordinary text, not a second hero. The bios can be names and role families, expanded on tap if you must, not five full essays before the brief repeats.

Nielsen Norman Group's finding still applies on a phone, often more so: people leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds are the judgment. A phone visit is easy to abandon. Do not ask for patience the research says you will not get.

Watch layout shift. If the headline jumps when the webfont arrives, or the button drops when the image loads, you have spent the buyer's trust on a twitch. Reserve space for the image. Use a font stack that does not reflow the role sentence. web.dev's description of Cumulative Layout Shift is the practical test: the page should not move under the finger. Google's threshold for a good score is under 0.1. You do not need to worship the number. You need the role line to stay where the eye put it.

## Speed is part of the brief

A slow first screen is a broken first screen. Largest Contentful Paint is the loading measure of the main content, and a good result is within 2.5 seconds. If your hero is a huge photograph of a lobby, you are asking the phone to download the wrong argument before it can show the role. Use a photograph that is the right subject and the right weight. Compress it. Do not ship the original export.

Interaction to Next Paint, within 200 milliseconds for a good score, is what the brief button feels like. If the button waits because a script is busy, the buyer taps twice and decides the form is broken. Keep the first view simple. A carousel, a chat widget, and an animation that runs before the sentence is readable are how a marketing site misses that threshold.

Test on a ordinary connection, not only on the office wireless. Load the page, lock the phone, unlock it, and see whether the role is there. If a consent banner covers the button, rewrite the banner so the role and the brief remain visible, or the banner has become the homepage.

## A review you can do in an afternoon

Use one phone and one person who hires and did not write the page.

1. Hand them the phone, locked, on the homepage.
2. Ask them to unlock it and say, within about ten seconds, what kind of role the firm fills and how they would start a brief.
3. If either answer is wrong, change the first screen before you discuss the sections below.
4. Then have them tap the brief and say whether the next screen matches the promise.
5. Rotate the phone. The role should still be readable. The button should still be tappable.

Do this again after any visual polish. Decoration has a habit of pushing the sentence down. A new typeface, a larger logo, a darker overlay: check the first view each time. The desktop review can happen after the phone review passes. Not before.

Write down the crop. If the meaningful part of the hero is missing, change the picture. Do not add a caption to explain a crop. The buyer will not read the caption in the first 10 seconds.

## Desktop is the second layout

When the phone holds the role and the brief, the wide screen can breathe. More of the workplace can show. A second column can hold a short refusal. The navigation can sit in a row instead of a menu. None of that is allowed to change the words. If the desktop headline is clever and the phone headline is clear, ship the clear one in both places. Cleverness that only fits on a wide monitor is a private joke.

Ask them to find the fee shape on the phone without help. If it takes a hunt through a menu, the narrow site is still a poster. One sentence on the fee is enough in the first scroll. A fee that exists only at desktop width will be missed by the buyer who never opens a laptop for this decision.

Do not maintain two copies of the truth. One role sentence. One action. One picture subject. The layouts differ. The claim does not.

After they can brief from the phone, the next screen has to say what happens. Read [what the contact path should promise after they reach out](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-recruiting-firm) before you send that button to a ten-field form.

If you want a second pair of eyes on the first screen of a phone, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the live page on a phone, not a desktop screenshot. The call is about what that screen proves.
